'''''Marsilea minuta''''', or '''dwarf waterclover''' is a [[species]] of [[aquatic plant|aquatic]] [[fern]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Marsileaceae]]. It is not to be confused with ''Marsilea minuta'' <small>[[Eugène Pierre Nicolas Fournier|E.Fourn.]] 1880</small>, which is a synonym for ''[[Marsilea vestita]]''.<ref name=Johnson>{{Cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=David M. |date=25 June 1986  |title=Systematics of the New World Species of Marsilea (Marsileaceae) |journal=Systematic Botany Monographs |language=English |location=Ann Arbor, MI |publisher=The American Society of Plant Taxonomists |publication-date=25 June 1986 |volume=11 |pages=39–40, 51, 63 |doi=10.2307/25027626 |isbn=978-0-912861-11-1 |issn=0737-8211 |jstor=25027626 |oclc=13455360 }}</ref>  Other [[common name]]s include '''gelid waterklawer''', '''small water clover''',<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> '''airy pepperwort''', and '''pepperwort''',<ref name=CABI>{{cite web |url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/32557 |title=Marsilea minuta (pepperwort) |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=15 May 2008  |website=Invasive Species Compendium |location=Wallingford, UK |publisher=CAB International |language=English |access-date=29 August 2017 }}</ref> though the lattermost also applies to plants in the genus [[Lepidium]].  In [[French language|French]] it is called ''{{lang|fr|marsilea à quatre feuilles}}'' ([[literal translation|literally]] "four-leafed marsilea")<ref name=CABI /> and ''{{lang|fr|petite marsilée}}'' (literally "little Marsilea"),<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> the latter appearing to be a [[calque]] with the [[Latin]] [[botanical name]].  In [[Chinese language|Chinese]] it is {{lang|zh|南国田字草}} ({{transliteration|zh|pinyin|nan guo tian zi cao}}),<ref name=China>{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Y. X. |last2=Johnson |first2=D. M. |date=6 June 2013  |editor1-last=Wu |editor1-first=Z. Y. |editor2-last=Raven |editor2-first=P. H. |editor3-last=Hong |editor3-first=D. Y. |title=Marsileaceae |url=http://flora.huh.harvard.edu/china/mss/volume02/Flora_of_China_Volume_2_3_Marsileaceae.pdf |access-date=25 August 2017 |journal=Flora of China |language=English |publication-date=6 June 2013 |volume=2-3 |pages=123–124 }}</ref> literally "southern field word grass," referencing the similarity of the [[Leaflet (botany)|leaflet]] shape to the [[Chinese characters|Chinese character]] for "field."  The [[Koch Rajbongshi people]] and [[Garo people]] call it ''{{lang|grt|shusni shak}}''.<ref name=Sarker>{{cite journal |last1=Sarker |first1=Sujan Kumer |last2=Hossain |first2=A.B.M. Enayet |date=June 2009  |title=Pteridophytes of Greater Mymensingh District of Bangladesh used as Vegetables and Medicines  |journal=Bangladesh Journal of Plant Taxonomy |language=English |publication-date=June 2009 |volume=16 |issue=1 |page=54 |doi=10.3329/bjpt.v16i1.2746 |issn=2224-7297 |citeseerx=10.1.1.606.3195 }}</ref> 
It is called '{{lang|bn|শুশনি শাক}}' ({{Lang|bn-Latn|shushni shak}}) in [[Bengali (language)|Bengali]]{{citation needed|date=February 2018}}. In parts of [[India]] it can be called ''{{lang|und|sunisanakka}}''.<ref name=Krishnamoorthy>{{cite book |date=6 April 2017  |chapter=34 Ayurveda and Yoga in the Management of Epilepsy |editor1-last=Krishnamoorthy |editor1-first=Ennapadam S. |editor2-last=Shorvon |editor2-first=Simon |editor3-last=Schachter |editor3-first=Steven |editor4-last=Misra |editor4-first=Vivek |title=Epilepsy: A Global Approach |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J_OkDgAAQBAJ&q=marislea&pg=PA160 |language=English |publisher=Cambridge University Press |publication-date=6 April 2017 |page=160 |doi=10.1017/9781139547918 |isbn=978-1-108-23215-9 |access-date=29 August 2017 }}</ref>  In [[Indonesian language|Indonesian]] it is ''{{lang|id|semanggi}}'' (literally "clover"),<ref name=CABI /> but this name also applies to ''[[Marsilea crenata]]''.  In [[Japanese language|Japanese]] it is {{transliteration|ja|nangokudenjiso}} and in [[Thai language|Thai]] it is {{transliteration|th|phakwaen}}.<ref name=CABI />  In [[Malaysian language|Malaysian]] it is ''{{lang|zsm|tapak itik}}'' (literally "duck footprints").<ref name=CABI />  In the [[Philippines]] it is ''{{lang|und|kaya-kayapuan}}'' (literally "so crowded").<ref name=CABI />

==Description==
''M. minuta'' has a  variable appearance,<ref name=Cook /> which often leads to confusion with closely related species.  In the water the plant is creeping and spreading, while on land it can appear cushion-like.<ref name=Cook />  It typically is [[perennial plant|perennial]] but sometimes appears [[Annual plant|annual]].  It is a [[tenagophyte]], with the juvenile growing [[Macrophyte#Submerged|submerged]] and the adult typically [[Terrestrial plant|terrestrial]].<ref name=Cook />

It has a light brown to green [[rhizome]] that is {{ convert | 0.4-0.8 | mm | inch | frac=64 }} thick with short tan hairs at the ends and internodal [[root]]s.<ref name=Johnson />  The land [[leaf|leaves]] are on erect, [[terete]], {{ convert | 5–13 | cm | inch }} long [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]].<ref name=Johnson />  The leaflets are {{ convert | 0.8-1.7 | cm | inch | frac=8 }} by {{ convert | 1.2–2 | cm | inch | frac=4 }}, mostly [[Glabrousness#In botany|glabrous]], [[Glossary of leaf morphology#cuneate|cuneate]] or [[Glossary of leaf morphology#flabellate|flabellate]].<ref name=Johnson />  The leaves in water are typically not floating, but emergent from the water.<ref name=Johnson />  Fertile leaves are produced on land with up to four [[Sporocarp (ferns)|sporocarp]]s each at [[Peduncle (botany)|penduncles]] near the base of the petiole.<ref name=Johnson />  It has a small sporocarp that is {{ convert | 2.6-4.1 | mm | inch | frac=64 }} long, {{ convert | 2.4-3.1 | mm | inch | frac=64 }} wide, and {{ convert | 1.3-1.7 | mm | inch | frac=64 }} thick.<ref name=Johnson /><ref name=FZ>{{cite web |url=http://apps.kew.org/efloras/namedetail.do?qry=namelist&flora=fz&taxon=7540&nameid=18883 |title=eFloras Results For Marsilea minuta |last=Schelpe |first=E. A. C. L. E. |year=1970 |series=Flora Zambesiaca |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |language=English |access-date=29 August 2017 }}</ref>  The sporocarp has a superior tooth at the apex of the stalk and an inferior tooth at the base.<ref name=Nagalingum>{{cite journal |last1=Nagalingum |first1=Nathalie S. |last2=Schneider |first2=Harald |last3=Pryer |first3=Kathleen M. |year=2007 |title=Molecular Phylogenetic Relationships and Morphological Evolution in the Heterosporous Fern Genus Marsilea  |journal=Systematic Botany |language=English |publication-date=2007 |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=16–25 |doi=10.1600/036364407780360256 |bibcode=2007SysBo..32...16N |s2cid=18310429 |issn=1548-2324 }}</ref><ref name=Cook />  The sporocarp has a conspicuous {{ convert | 1.5-2.2 | mm | inch | frac=64 }} long [[raphe]],<ref name=Johnson /><ref name=Nagalingum /> about two-thirds the length of the sporocarp and semi-terete.<ref name=Cook />  Unlike a few ''[[Marsilea]]'' species, ''M. minuta'' sporocarps mature above ground.<ref name=Nagalingum />

==Taxonomy==
''M. minuta'' is thought to be closely related to ''[[Marsilea quadrifolia]]''.<ref name=Johnson />  [[Molecular biology|Molecular]] [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetic]] analysis of the genus ''[[Marsilea]]'' puts both in a widespread [[Old World]] subgroup also called "Marsilea" along with ''[[Marsilea angustifolia|M. angustifolia]]'', ''[[Marsilea drummondii|M. drummondii]]'', ''[[Marsilea crenata|M. crenata]]'', and ''[[Marsilea fadeniana|M. fadeniana]]'' and indicating that ''M. crenata'' is actually a synonym of ''M. minuta''.<ref name=Nagalingum /><ref name=CABI />

==Habitat and ecology==
''Marsilea minuta'' can grow from [[sea level]] up to {{Convert|1950|m|abbr=on}} in [[elevation]]<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" /> in [[pond]]s and other shallow water.<ref name=China />  It can grow in [[fresh water]] or [[brackish water]] in [[clay]] or [[sand]]y [[Soil classification|soil]].<ref name=Johnson />  The plant can develop into large [[Colony (biology)|colonies]], and can be [[weed]]y.<ref name=Johnson /><ref name=FZ />  Some of its preferred habitat is being lost to [[agriculture]] but as it readily grows in [[Paddy field]]s, [[Drainage system (agriculture)|drainage]] [[ditch]]es, and other marginal areas its overall population is stable.<ref name="iucn status 19 November 2021" />  It has the potential to be [[Invasive species|invasive]] and dispersal through [[aquarium]] trade and other human means should be limited.<ref name=CABI />

The leaves and sporocarps of ''M. minuta'' are eaten by many [[Anseriformes|waterfowl]] species, and the intact sporocarps pass through undigested to be spread to new areas.<ref name=CABI />  [[Elophila responsalis]] also feeds on the leaves, but is not thought to do much damage to the plant.<ref name=CABI />

The plant is susceptible to [[herbicide]]s such as [[bensulfuron-methyl]], [[cinosulfuron]], [[2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid|2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid]], [[oxyfluorfen]], and [[paraquat]].<ref name=CABI />  Otherwise it can tolerate high levels of organic pollution.<ref name=Cook />

==Uses==
It is eaten in [[India]], [[Sri Lanka]],<ref name=Terra>{{cite book |last1=Terra |first1=G.J.A. |year=1966 |chapter=IIID Ferns and Related Plants |title=Tropical vegetables: vegetable growing in the tropics and subtropics especially of indigenous vegetables |series=Communication |language=English |volume=54e |edition=1st |location=Amsterdam |publisher=Koninklijk Instituut voor de Tropen |publication-date=1966 |page=57 |oclc=9027279 |quote=Marsilea minuta L. (Marsileaceae) I Ce (3.3%) }}</ref> and in [[Bangladesh]].<ref name=Sarker />  In [[China]] it is used as [[forage]].<ref name=China />  It has a raw protein content of 3.3%.<ref name=Terra />

The plant is used [[Traditional Chinese medicine|traditionally]] in China for [[edema]], [[Wound|skin injuries]], [[snakebite]], and [[inflammation]].<ref name=China />  In [[Mymensingh District]] it is [[Traditional medicine|traditionally]] used to treat [[cough]], [[headache]], [[hypertension]], [[sleep disorder]]s, and [[respiratory disease]]s.<ref name=Sarker />  It is combined with ''[[Nardostachys jatamansi]]'' and after development by [[Asima Chatterjee]]<ref name="Basak">{{cite journal |last1=Basak |first1=Swati |title=Women, Science, Education And Empowerment: Asima Chatterjee, The Genius Lady |journal=IMPACT: International Journal of Research in Humanities, Arts and Literature |date=May 2015 |volume=3 |issue=5 |pages=133–138 |url=http://oaji.net/articles/2015/488-1434793998.pdf}}</ref> sold as an [[Ayurveda|ayurvedic]] treatment for [[epilepsy]] called Ayush-56.<ref name=Krishnamoorthy />  However, Ayush-56 does not show encouraging results in treating the disease.<ref name=Tripathi>{{cite journal |last1=Tripathi |first1=M |last2=Maheshwari |first2=MC |last3=Jain |first3=S |last4=Padma |first4=MV |year=2000|title=Ayurvedic Medicine and Epilepsy |url=http://www.neurology-asia.org/articles/20001_001.pdf |access-date=29 August 2017 |journal=Neurology Journal of Southeast Asia |language=English |publication-date=2000 |volume=5 |pages=1–4 }}</ref> It is also used as a phytoremediator of arsenic while growing with rice plants.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hassi|first1=Ummehani|last2=Hossain|first2=Md. Tawhid|last3=Huq|first3=S. M. Imamul|date=2017-10-10|title=Mitigating arsenic contamination in rice plants with an aquatic fern, Marsilea minuta|journal=Environmental Monitoring and Assessment|language=en|volume=189|issue=11|page=550|doi=10.1007/s10661-017-6270-2|pmid=29018967|bibcode=2017EMnAs.189..550H |s2cid=36716267|issn=0167-6369}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hassi|first1=U|last2=Hossain|first2=MT|last3=Huq|first3=SMI|date=2018-07-08|title=Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium status of rice co-planted with a novel phytoremediator, Marsilea minuta L.|journal=Bangladesh Journal of Agricultural Research|volume=43|issue=2|pages=211–218|doi=10.3329/bjar.v43i2.37326|issn=2408-8293|doi-access=free|url=https://biblio.ugent.be/publication/01GT6GEARW0D2AK0N7H74EAYTR/file/01GT6GKDT7GAPKM4W78RBQT0NW.pdf}}</ref>
